subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Pie chart interpretation; degrees vs percent, sector calculation

questions.stem: A pie chart shows monthly expenditure of ₹50,000. Food = 36° sector. Amount spent on food is:
questions.explanation: Pie chart total = 360°. Fraction = 36°/360° = 1/10 = 10%. Food = 10% × 50,000 = ₹5,000. Distractor 4 = 36 × 100 = wrong. Always: degrees → percent (÷ 3.6 or × 100/360); percent → degrees (× 3.6).
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: In a pie chart, 25% data is shown for one item. The corresponding angle is:
questions.explanation: 25% of 360° = 90°. Quick reckoner: 10% = 36°; 25% = 90°; 33.3% = 120°; 50% = 180°; 75% = 270°. Distractors are common alternative percent → angle conversions.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: Pie chart shows: A = 90°, B = 120°, C = 75°, D = 75°. If total income is ₹72,000, B's share is:
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A class budget pie chart shows: Books 30%, Stationery 20%, Library 15%, Sports 25%, Misc 10%. Books spend ₹6000. Total budget is:
questions.explanation: 30% = 6000 → 1% = 200 → 100% = 20,000. Total = ₹20,000. Distractor 15,000 = used 40% wrongly. Distractor 25/30k = arithmetic slips.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: (Same class budget data, total ₹20,000.) Amount spent on Library is:
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: Pie chart of student strength by stream: Science 40%, Commerce 30%, Arts 20%, Vocational 10%. If Arts has 80 students, total students:
questions.explanation: Arts 20% = 80 → 1% = 4 → 100% = 400. Total = 400 students. Verify: Science 40% = 160; Commerce 30% = 120; Arts 20% = 80; Voc 10% = 40. Sum 400 ✓.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A pie chart represents the distribution of 2,400 employees across 6 departments. The Production department's sector subtends an angle of 90°. How many employees belong to departments other than Production?

options.option_text: 600 employees counted in the Production sector
1,800 employees across the remaining five departments
2,100 employees spread across the other departments

questions.explanation: Production = (90/360) × 2400 = 600 employees. Employees outside Production = 2400 − 600 = 1,800. Option A (600) is the Production count itself — the classic 'find the sector, not its complement' trap.

questions.stem: A pie chart shows the area distribution across 4 zones of a city. Zone P occupies 90°, Zone Q occupies 72°, and Zone R occupies 108°. What is the central angle for Zone S?

options.option_text: 72°, matching Zone Q's share of the city area
90°, the residual angle completing the full circle
108°, equal to the largest zone already allocated
54°, one-sixth of the complete 360° pie circle

questions.explanation: All sectors must sum to 360°. Zone S = 360 − 90 − 72 − 108 = 90°. Option C (108°) would push the total to 378°, which exceeds 360°. Option D (54°) incorrectly assumes equal division into six parts.

questions.stem: Two pie charts show workforce data for Factory X (total 1,500 workers) and Factory Y (total 2,000 workers). The 'Skilled Workers' sector is 120° in Factory X's chart and 90° in Factory Y's chart. What is the difference in skilled workers between the two factories?

options.option_text: Factory X has 250 more skilled workers than Y
Both factories have exactly the same skilled worker count
Factory Y has 250 more skilled workers than X
Factory X has 125 fewer skilled workers than Y

questions.explanation: Factory X skilled = (120/360) × 1500 = 500; Factory Y skilled = (90/360) × 2000 = 500. Both equal 500 — the smaller angle in Y is exactly offset by its larger workforce. Option A is the most tempting error: comparing angles directly without scaling by base totals.

questions.stem: In a pie chart of a company's annual revenue, the sectors for Electronics, FMCG, and Pharma together span 240° and are in the ratio 5 : 4 : 3. What is the central angle allocated to the Electronics sector?

options.option_text: 60°, assigned to the smallest ratio component
100°, proportional to 5 parts of the 240° arc
150°, computed as 5 parts out of the full 360°
80°, the angle that belongs to the FMCG segment

questions.explanation: Total ratio parts = 5+4+3 = 12. Electronics = (5/12) × 240 = 100°. Option C (150°) is the classic error of applying the ratio to 360° instead of the stated 240°. Option D (80°) is FMCG's correct angle: (4/12) × 240 = 80°.

questions.stem: A pie chart shows five states' share of national wheat production: State A = 28%, State B = 22%, State C = 18%, State D = 16%, State E = 16%. If total production is 450 lakh tonnes, by how many lakh tonnes does State A exceed State C?

options.option_text: 50 lakh tonnes, after rounding to the nearest figure

questions.explanation: Gap = 28% − 18% = 10%. Excess = 10% of 450 = 45 lakh tonnes. Option A (36 lt) uses 8%, which equals the gap between A and B, not A and C. Option D (54 lt) uses 12%, the gap between A and D — a common misread of the chart.

questions.stem: Two pie charts represent the budgets of State X (₹800 crore total) and State Y (₹600 crore total). The Education sector occupies 135° in State X's chart and 150° in State Y's chart. What is the ratio of Education expenditure of State X to that of State Y?

options.option_text: 9 : 10, derived by comparing the two sector angles directly
6 : 5, after converting sector angles to crore amounts
4 : 3, obtained by scaling the total budgets alone
5 : 6, arrived at by reversing the computed ratio

questions.explanation: State X Education = (135/360) × 800 = (3/8) × 800 = ₹300 cr. State Y Education = (150/360) × 600 = (5/12) × 600 = ₹250 cr. Ratio = 300 : 250 = 6 : 5. Option A (9:10) is the most seductive error — it treats the sector angles as the ratio, completely ignoring that the two base totals differ.

questions.stem: A pie chart shows the composition of a 720-member parliamentary committee: General 35%, OBC 30%, SC 20%, ST 10%, EWS 5%. A sub-committee is formed using ALL SC and ST members plus 60 newly inducted EWS members (no other categories). EWS members constitute what fraction of this sub-committee?

options.option_text: 4/13, counting all original and inducted EWS members
2/15, dividing total EWS by the original 720-member body
5/23, adding only the 60 new EWS and ignoring original 36
1/6, dividing original EWS only by SC-plus-ST total alone

questions.explanation: SC = 20% of 720 = 144; ST = 10% of 720 = 72; original EWS = 5% of 720 = 36; total EWS in sub-committee = 36 + 60 = 96. Sub-committee size = 144 + 72 + 96 = 312. Fraction = 96/312 = 4/13. Option B (2/15) mistakenly uses the original 720 as denominator. Option C (5/23) forgets the pre-existing 36 EWS members: 60/(144+72+60) = 60/276 = 5/23.
